title: Cell Wall
summary: The cell wall is the sturdy outer shell of plant cells (and of fungi and many bacteria) - a rigid layer outside the cell membrane that gives the cell support, protection, and shape. Explore how it works with the membrane and vacuole to keep a plant standing.

compareCandidate.label: Cell wall vs. cell membrane
compareCandidate.description: The cell wall is a thick, rigid, non-living shell that gives support and shape - only in plants, fungi, and many bacteria. The membrane is a thin, flexible, living layer in ALL cells that controls what enters and leaves.

processes: Giving the cell a fixed rectangular shape
Working with the vacuole to keep plants firm
plainLanguageExplanation: The cell wall is a thick, rigid layer that wraps around the outside of plant cells, just beyond the cell membrane. It is mostly made of a tough carbohydrate called cellulose. Its job is to support and protect the cell and give it its fixed shape, like a strong brick wall around a room. The wall is porous, so water and dissolved materials can still pass through, and the membrane inside keeps controlling what enters the cell. Plants, fungi, and many bacteria have cell walls; animal cells do not.

keyFacts.label: Works with
keyFacts.value: The full central vacuole presses on the wall to hold the cell firm

whyItMatters: The cell wall is what lets plants stand tall and survive tough conditions - it supports every plant cell and protects it. Understanding it explains why plants are firm, why wood is strong, and why plant cells are shaped differently from animal cells.
tagline: The sturdy shell of the plant cell
didYouKnow: Wood is basically thousands of empty plant cell walls - the strong carbohydrate cellulose is what makes trees so hard.
